title: Not for the reward (Avot 1:3)
hookLine: Antigonus: be like servants who serve without thought of a reward
tomorrow: Sit in the dust of the wise

cards: Badges. Employee of the month. The world runs on little rewards, and to be fair, they work.
Plenty of people learned to read for a sticker. But watch what can happen when the reward stops. The kid who read for stickers stops reading.
The volunteer who wanted to be thanked quits when nobody does. Long ago, a sage named Antigonus, from a town called Socho, looked at this and gave advice that's hard to hear.

teach.b: Antigonus received the tradition from Simon the Just, the next link in the chain. His saying, in paraphrase: don't be like servants who serve their master in order to receive a reward.
Be like servants who serve their master not in order to receive a reward. And let the awe of heaven be upon you.
The word for reward here is peras. Some commentators say it means something small: a tip, a treat, a little bonus a master tosses to a servant. Antigonus isn't saying good deeds go unrewarded.
He's saying don't make the tip the point. Do the right thing because it's right, and because of who you're serving.
An old story shows how easily this can be misheard. Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early companion to Avot, tells of two students of Antigonus, Zadok and Boethus.
They heard, don't serve for a reward, and concluded: then there is no reward, no world to come. And, the story says, they broke away and founded their own sects.
Historians doubt the story, but the warning is clear: a saying about motive can be twisted into a saying about emptiness. Later, the philosopher Maimonides made peace with the gold stars.
A child, he wrote, is taught first with sweets, then with new clothes, then with coins, and later with honor.
That's fine. That's how people start. The goal is to grow, slowly, toward serving out of love: for the one you serve, and for the good itself.

how: The Talmud teaches that a person should keep doing the commandments even for other motives, because from that they come to do them lishmah, for their own sake.

o: a fair wage owed for a full day's work
a small tip or bonus given as a reward
a punishment for a servant who fails

games.q: the saying and its readers — tap the pairs.
p: misheard it as no reward at all
from sweets toward serving out of love

s: Antigonus taught that good deeds have no reward
he said not to serve for the reward. an old story says two students misheard it that way.
Antigonus received the tradition from Simon the Just
he's the next link in Avot's chain.
Maimonides said it's wrong to start learning for rewards
he said children begin with sweets and coins, and grow toward serving from love.

games.q: you're a student of Antigonus. your teacher says: don't serve your master for the reward. what do you conclude?
o: then there is no reward at all.
do the right thing for its own sake, whatever comes.
serve only masters who don't pay.
games.why: Antigonus meant: don't make the reward the point. an old story says two students, Zadok and Boethus, concluded there was no reward, and broke away.

practice: Look over the good things you did this week and notice, honestly, which had a little tip attached: a thank-you you were waiting for, a like, a favor owed. That's human, so don't scold yourself.
Then think of one thing you could do today where no tip is possible, where no one will know and no one will thank you.

wordCard.voice: Peras. A reward, a small tip: the word in Antigonus's warning not to serve like a servant who expects one, but with awe of heaven.

orig.note: Hebrew: in order to receive a reward. The motive Antigonus warns against (Avot 1:3).

carryVoice: Your line: not for the prize. The sweets are only where it starts. Until tomorrow.
